Part 1 · Fundamentals

What chemistry and physics decide how a suspension PVC batch behaves?

Part 1 · the plan

Five ideas that explain every trend on the console

  1. Free-radical chain growththe rate law and its heat
  2. Two initiators and the gel effectwhy the heat release rises to a peak
  3. Where the monomer sitsflat pressure, then the end-point drop
  4. Heat balance and runawaywhy the reactor needs control and cooling margin
  5. Temperature sets the gradethe K-value and the ±0.5 °C band

Chemistry

One reaction, one large heat of reaction

Everything the operator does in R-101 is about removing the heat of this one reaction.

$$n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCl}\;\longrightarrow\;\left(\mathrm{-CH_2-CHCl-}\right)_n\qquad \Delta H_p=-71\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$$
VCM
vinyl chloride monomer, $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCl}$, boils at −13 °C
62.5 g/mol
PVC
poly(vinyl chloride), the polymer; insoluble in its own monomer
1.40 t/m³
$\Delta H_p$
heat released per mole of VCM polymerised
kJ/mol

$71\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}\div 62.5\ \mathrm{g/mol}=1.14\ \mathrm{MJ}$ per kg of PVC made.

Free-radical chain growth

Three elementary steps

$\mathrm{I}\xrightarrow{k_d}2\,\mathrm{R^\bullet}$ peroxide initiator splits into two radicals
$\mathrm{R^\bullet}+\mathrm{M}\xrightarrow{k_p}\mathrm{R^\bullet}$ each radical adds monomer, chain grows
$\mathrm{R^\bullet}+\mathrm{R^\bullet}\xrightarrow{k_t}\mathrm{P}$ two radicals meet, chain stops
$\mathrm{I},\ \mathrm{M},\ \mathrm{R^\bullet},\ \mathrm{P}$
initiator, monomer, growing radical, dead polymer
mol/L
$k_d,\ k_p,\ k_t$
rate constants: decomposition, propagation, termination
s⁻¹; L·mol⁻¹·s⁻¹

Deriving the rate of polymerisation

Radicals are made as fast as they diestep 1 of 2

Radicals live under a second, so their concentration settles almost instantly: the quasi-steady-state assumption.

$\dfrac{d[\mathrm{R^\bullet}]}{dt}=2fk_d[\mathrm{I}]-2k_t[\mathrm{R^\bullet}]^2\approx 0$ radicals made minus radicals terminated
$[\mathrm{R^\bullet}]=\sqrt{\dfrac{f\,k_d[\mathrm{I}]}{k_t}}$ solve the balance for the radical level
$f$
initiator efficiency: share of radicals that start a chain
–

Deriving the rate of polymerisation

The classical rate lawstep 2 of 2

From step 1$[\mathrm{R^\bullet}]=\sqrt{f\,k_d[\mathrm{I}]/k_t}$
$R_p=k_p[\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{R^\bullet}]$ monomer is used almost only by propagation
$$R_p=k_p[\mathrm{M}]\sqrt{\dfrac{f\,k_d[\mathrm{I}]}{k_t}}$$

Rate ∝ monomer × square root of the radical supply.

Holds while $k_t$ is constant — true only at low conversion (see gel effect).

The radical supply

Half-life tells how long an initiator lasts

$t_{1/2}$
time for half the initiator to decompose (supplier data at 57 °C)
h
$E_a$
activation energy of decomposition, 120 in this model
kJ/mol
$T$
reactor temperature, absolute in the exponent
K
$$k_d=\frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}\qquad k_d(T)=k_{d,57}\exp\!\left[-\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}-\frac{1}{330.15}\right)\right]$$

R-101 uses a fast initiator A ($t_{1/2}$ 1.5 h) and a slow B (12 h), charged 1 : 0.5.

Interactive — drag the sliders

Why a fast + slow initiator pair

Rate with gel effect$r_p\propto\sqrt{k_{dA}I_A+k_{dB}I_B}\,(1+5X)$
$t_{1/2}$ of A / Btime to $X_f$: pair / A onlypeak heat: pair / A only

■ A + B   ■ A only   heat released, same fast-initiator charge

The slow initiator keeps radicals coming while the gel effect builds: the pair reaches $X_f$ about 0.7 h sooner, at the price of a higher peak.

Beyond the classical rate law

The gel effect speeds the reaction up

The rate law assumed a constant $k_t$. Inside a swollen PVC particle, long chains can hardly move.

$$r_p=k_X\,M_0\,\sqrt{R}\;g(X),\qquad g=1+Q\,X\quad(X\lt X_f)$$
$X$
conversion: fraction of the charged VCM turned into PVC
–
$M_0,\ R$
VCM charged; radical supply $\sum k_{d,i}I_i$
kmol; s⁻¹
$g,\ Q$
gel factor; its strength (Q = 5 here)
–

Termination slows, radicals accumulate: this is the OTS model's lumped form, valid up to $X_f$.

Two phases inside every droplet

PVC does not dissolve in VCM — it swells

$$w=\frac{m_{VCM}}{m_{VCM}+m_{PVC}}=1-X$$

$w$: VCM mass fraction in a droplet; $m$: mass, t.

$1-X_f=0.28\Rightarrow X_f=0.72$ gel saturates at 28 wt % VCM

$X_f$: conversion where the last free liquid VCM disappears.

Why the pressure tells the phase

Pressure = monomer activity × vapour pressure

$$P=a\,P^{sat}_{VCM}(T)+P^{sat}_{w}(T)+p_{in},\qquad \ln a=\ln\phi+(1-\phi)+\chi(1-\phi)^2$$
$a$
VCM activity: 1 while free VCM exists, below 1 once only gel is left
–
$\phi$
VCM volume fraction in the swollen gel
–
$\chi$
Flory–Huggins interaction parameter, fitted so $a=1$ at 28 wt %
–
$p_{in}$
partial pressure of inerts (N₂, air left after evacuation)
bar

At 57 °C: 9.22 (VCM) + 0.18 (water) + 0.23 (inerts) − 1.01 = 8.62 bar g.

Interactive — the end-point signal

Flat pressure, then a drop

Pressure equation$P=a\,P^{sat}_{VCM}+P^{sat}_{w}+p_{in}$
activity $a$pressuredrop below running max

Simplified: ignores VCM dissolved in water and vapour, so it reads about 1 % conversion late.

Below $X_f$ the pressure cannot see conversion; the 1.8 bar drop after $X_f$ marks ≈ 85 % conversion — the end point.

Energy balance on the contents

Temperature moves only when heat does not balance

$$m\,c_p\frac{dT}{dt}=\underbrace{\Delta H_p\,r_p}_{Q_{rx}}+W_{ag}-Q_j-Q_b-Q_c$$
$m\,c_p$
heat capacity of water + VCM + PVC in R-101
kJ/K
$Q_{rx},\ W_{ag}$
heat of polymerisation; agitator work into the slurry
kW
$Q_j,\ Q_b,\ Q_c$
heat removed by jacket, baffles, reflux condenser E-101
kW

At 2 h: 2.71 + 0.28 ≈ 1.50 + 0.40 + 0.97 (+ 0.1 to warm injected water) MW.

Interactive — generation vs removal

Why the reactor is open-loop unstable

Generation and removal$Q_{gen}\approx Q_0e^{0.086(T-57)}$
$Q_{rem}=UA\,(T-T_c)$
balance points

■ generated   ■ removed   ● stable   ○ unstable

Generation rises ≈ 9 %/°C, removal ≈ 4–5 %/°C: 57 °C is an unstable balance point that only the controller holds.

Interactive — temperature sets the grade

The K-value remembers the whole batch

$$K=67-0.62\,(T-57),\qquad \bar K=\frac{1}{X}\int_0^X K\,dX$$

K-value: chain-length index of PVC (from solution viscosity).

batch K-value (on grade 66–68)

A 2 °C error over half the batch moves K by 0.6 — one careless hour can put a whole batch off grade.

Part 1 · summary

What Part 1 settled

  • Heat = 1.14 MJ per kg PVC; rate ∝ monomer × √(radical supply) × gel factor.
  • A fast + slow initiator pair keeps the heat release from fading.
  • Pressure is flat until $X_f=0.72$, then falls: the end point.
  • Generation outruns removal above 57 °C: control and margin are essential.
  • Temperature fixes the K-value: hold ±0.5 °C all batch.

Design basis

Numbers for the four-reactor plantstep 2 of 2

From step 1$P_a=N\,m_{PVC}\,H/t_c,\qquad m_{PVC}=X_{end}\,m_{VCM}$
$m_{PVC}=0.848\times 51=43.2\ \mathrm{t}$ reference batch end point

Interactive — capacity planner

What sets the plant output?

plant capacity, kt/y

PVC per batchaverage heat, all reactors

The OTS runs a batch in ≈ 7.7 h (charge 1.4 h + react 5.3 h + empty 1.1 h): shaving the cycle is worth as much as a bigger reactor.

Which heat sizes the coolers?

Design for the peak, not the average

7.9 MW is shared by four reactors over a cycle. Coolers must carry one reactor at its worst moment.

Basis (one reactor, reference batch)Heat
Plant average ÷ 4 reactors (whole cycle)1.98 MW
Average while reacting: 49.1 gigajoule (GJ) ÷ 5.27 h2.59 MW
Peak release near $X\approx0.72$3.43 MW
Peak + agitator work, to be removed≈ 3.7 MW

Scale-up

Volume grows as $D^3$, jacket area only as $D^2$

$D,\ H$
vessel diameter; tangent-to-tangent height (4.5 m, 7.4 m)
m
$A_j$
wetted jacket area (119 m² at 83 % level)
m²
$U$
overall heat-transfer coefficient through the wall
kW·m⁻²·K⁻¹
$V\approx1.55\,D^3,\quad A_j\propto D^2$ fixed shape: $H/D=1.64$, 2:1 heads
$\dfrac{Q_j}{Q_{rx}}=\dfrac{U A_j\,\Delta T}{q_v V}\propto\dfrac{1}{D}$ heat made per m³ is fixed by chemistry

$q_v$: heat released per m³ of contents. Bigger vessel → smaller share cooled by the jacket.

Interactive — grow the vessel

When does the jacket run out?

Scale-up rule$Q_j/Q_{rx}\propto 1/D$
diameterjacket areaE-101 must carry

same shape, same wall ΔT and U as R-101; peak heat ∝ volume

Above ≈ 20 m³ jacket + baffles cannot carry the peak: the jacket runs out as the vessel grows, so a condenser adds the missing area.

Reflux condenser E-101

A condensing side at constant temperature

$\dot m_w\,c_p$
cooling-water capacity rate through the tubes
kW/K
$UA_c$
condenser conductance, 130 kW/K clean
kW/K
$b$
fraction of tubes blanketed by inert gas
–
$\varepsilon$
effectiveness: actual ÷ maximum possible duty
–
$$Q_c=\varepsilon\,\dot m_wc_p\,(T_{cond}-T_{w,in}),\qquad \varepsilon=1-\exp\!\left[-\frac{UA_c(1-b)}{\dot m_wc_p}\right]$$

Valid because VCM condenses at a single temperature (≈ reactor temperature).

Interactive — size the water

More water, or fewer inerts?

Effectiveness$Q_c=\varepsilon\dot m_wc_p(T_{cond}-T_{w,in})$

E-101 duty

effectiveness εCW returnmaximum at 540 m³/h

Past ≈ 150 m³/h extra water buys little, while 50 % blanketing halves the ceiling: vent inerts before adding water.

Agitator M-101

Power keeps droplets small and the wall film thin

$N_p$
impeller power number (≈ constant in turbulent flow)
–
$N,\ d$
impeller speed; impeller diameter
s⁻¹; m
$$P_{ag}=N_p\,\rho\,N^3d^5\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{P_{ag}}{V}=\frac{290\ \mathrm{kW}}{140\ \mathrm{m^3}}\approx 2\ \mathrm{kW/m^3}$$

Matches the vendor table: 20 000 gal (76 m³) with 200 hp (149 kW), two impellers.

Agitator work (≈ 0.28 MW) enters the heat balance as heat.

Part 2 · summary

What Part 2 settled

  • 4 × 140 m³ reactors, 43.2 t PVC per batch, 6.9 h cycle → 200 kt/y, 7.9 MW average.
  • Coolers are sized for the peak: ≈ 3.7 MW per reactor.
  • Jacket share falls as 1/D; above ≈ 20 m³ a reflux condenser is needed.
  • E-101 duty is limited by water capacity and by inert blanketing.
  • Design 15.2 bar g, PSV 15 bar g, trips at 63 °C and 12.5 bar g.

Reference runs in the OTS

A batch cycle of about 7.7 hours

Cleaning and inspection add to this; the design basis assumed 6.9 h with overlapped charging.

Virtual lab — walk through the reference batch

What the batch looks like hour by hour

phaseconversion $X$pressureheat releasedjacket / baffles / E-101E-101 water

■ heat released, MW   ■ E-101 duty   ■ pressure, bar g

The jacket stays near 1.5 MW all batch; E-101 absorbs the rise to the 3.4 MW peak, then the pressure falls to the end point.

Before the initiator

Order matters: air out, water in, then monomer

  1. Jacket pump and baffle water on; evacuate below 0.05 bar a.
  2. 60 t water at 55 °C with the PVA pot open.
  3. Agitator on once the lower impeller is covered.
  4. 51 t VCM; the mixture settles near 46 °C, 6.5 bar g.
  5. Heat the jacket loop on steam to 54 °C, then cascade.

PVA: poly(vinyl alcohol), the suspending agent that keeps droplets apart.

Starting the reaction

Initiate at temperature, with the jacket already cool

  • Charge initiator at TI-100 ≥ 56.8 °C and jacket inlet below 62 °C.
  • Put VPC-130 and FIC-130 on control at once; vent inerts 4 min.
  • Heat release climbs to ≈ 2 MW in 20 minutes.
E-101 brought inPeak TI-101Max TV-110B
At initiation58.2 °C47 %
At 3 % conversion58.6 °C100 %

Interactive — the early-batch squeeze

Why the jacket must carry the start

Anti-foam clamp on FIC-130$F_{130}\le 12\,X_{I}\ \ \mathrm{m^3/h}$
heat releasedE-101 water allowedE-101 duty allowedjacket must carry

In the first 1–2 % the clamp keeps E-101 small: the jacket carries the start, E-101 takes over as conversion builds.

Through the peak (X ≈ 0.6–0.75)

Watch the margin, not only the temperature

At 57 °C the balance is unstable (Part 1). What keeps it held is spare cooling.

  • VPC-130 keeps TV-110B near 50 %: jacket margin both ways.
  • TV-110B at 100 % and E-101 at maximum: margin is gone.
  • TI-132 falling: inerts blanket E-101 — vent with HIC-135.
  • No margin and rising temperature: short-stop, do not wait for 63 °C.

From end point to empty vessel

Stop, recover the monomer, discharge

  1. PD-100 reaches 1.8 bar (≈ 85 %): inject short-stop within minutes.
  2. Stop shrinkage water: LIC-100 and FIC-103 to manual, closed.
  3. Degas to VCM recovery through XV-105 + HIC-105 to 2 bar g (≈ 32 min).
  4. Close XV-105, open the N₂ pad (1.5 bar g).
  5. Discharge to D-102 with the agitator running (≈ 29 min).

PD-100: pressure drop below the running maximum. N₂ pad pushes slurry out without air.

Safety

Why VCM is handled in a closed system

Toxic

Known human carcinogen: exposure limits are around 1 ppm.

Flammable

Flammable in air at about 3.6–33 vol %; evacuation removes air first.

Volatile

Boils at −13 °C: every vent goes to recovery, never to air.

Part 3 · summary

What Part 3 settled

  • OTS cycle ≈ 7.7 h: 1.4 h charge and heat-up, 5.3 h reaction, 1.1 h to empty.
  • Evacuate, water + PVA, agitate, then VCM; initiate hot with a cool jacket.
  • E-101 on control from initiation; the foam clamp limits it early.
  • Hold 57 °C by watching margin; short-stop before the SIS must.
  • End point 1.8 bar → short-stop → degas to 2 bar g → discharge under N₂.

Part 4 · summary

What Part 4 settled

  • Recipe: 60 t water + PVA, 51 t VCM, initiators 1 : 0.5, ≈ 22 t shrinkage water.
  • At 2 h: 57 °C, 8.62 bar g, 26 %, 2.71 MW released.
  • 51 t VCM → 43.2 t PVC + 7.8 t to recovery; slurry ≈ 34 wt % PVC.
  • Jacket removes half the batch heat, E-101 a third, baffles the rest.

Piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&ID), sheets 001 and 002

Drag the drawing to pan. Jump to:

Sheet 001 carries the reactor, charges, vents and SIS; sheet 002 carries every heat-removal loop.

The most important loop

TIC-100 sets the jacket; TIC-110 makes it happen

The drawings show the hardware. The strategy that holds 57 °C starts with one cascade.

The slave rejects steam or CW upsets before the reactor feels them.

Tuning: TIC-100 gain 12, reset 900 s, rate 120 s; TIC-110 gain 2, reset 40 s.

Interactive — one output, two valves

Split range: steam below 50 %, cooling water above

$$\mathrm{TV\text{-}110A}=2\,(50-u)^+$$$$\mathrm{TV\text{-}110B}=2\,(u-50)^+$$

$u$: TIC-110 output, % · $(\,)^+$ means negatives count as 0.

TV-110A steam (fail closed)TV-110B cooling water (fail open)jacket is

At 50 % both valves shut: one controller heats at start-up and cools during the reaction without switching modes.

VPC-130 → FIC-130

Keep the jacket valve mid-range; let E-101 take the rest

  • VPC-130 measures TV-110B demand, set point 50 %.
  • Demand above 50 %: more E-101 water; below: less.
  • Slow on purpose (reset 900 s) so it never fights TIC-100.
  • Clamped to 12 m³/h per % XI-100 against foam.

VPC: valve-position controller. FIC-130 sits in cascade under it.

Part 5 · summary

What Part 5 settled

  • Sheet 001: reactor, charges, vents, SIS; sheet 002: heat removal.
  • TIC-100 → TIC-110 cascade with split range steam / CW.
  • VPC-130 holds TV-110B near 50 % by moving E-101 water.

  • Permissives block VCM, initiator and discharge until safe.

Staying ahead

Alarms, trends and simulation speed

Alarms

Newest unacknowledged first; horn until silenced. Unacknowledged over 60 s costs score.

Trends

Groups or the selected loop's PV, SP and OUT; windows 5–60 min.

Time

Freeze to think; speed up to 200× for the long parts.

Typical suspension PVC plant

R-101 is one step in a longer line

Only R-101 is simulated in this OTS; the rest is shown for context.

VCM recovery

Compress, then condense what the vapour pressure allows

Degassing sends ≈ 7.8 t VCM per batch to recovery at 1–2 bar a. To reuse it, it must become liquid again.

$P,\ T_c$
condenser pressure; condensing temperature
bar a; °C
$y_{out}$
VCM mole fraction left in the vent gas
–
$$y_{out}=\frac{P^{sat}_{VCM}(T_c)}{P}\qquad\text{(saturated vent)}$$

Inerts leave with $y_{out}$ of VCM; the vent goes to incineration.

Interactive — recovery condenser

How much VCM condenses?

Saturated vent$y_{out}=P^{sat}_{VCM}(T_c)/P$

of the VCM recovered as liquid

$P^{sat}_{VCM}(T_c)$VCM in vent gas

Higher pressure and colder water both help, but inerts always carry some VCM out — keep air out of the reactor.

Slurry stripping

Steam strips the VCM left inside the grains

$N$
equilibrium stages (trays) in the stripping column
–
$S$
stripping factor = $K\,V/L$, steam's capacity versus slurry flow
–
$\varphi$
fraction of VCM left in the stripped slurry
–
$$\varphi=\frac{S-1}{S^{N+1}-1}\qquad\text{(Kremser)}$$

Illustrative: real columns are limited by diffusion out of the grains, not only equilibrium.

Interactive — size a stripper

Stages or steam?

Kremser$\varphi=(S-1)/(S^{N+1}-1)$

VCM left in the stripped slurry, ppm (on PVC)

Each stage multiplies the reduction by $S$: with $S$ near 1 no number of trays helps; with $S\approx2$ a dozen trays reach ppm.

From slurry to powder

Take the water off mechanically first

Decanter centrifuge

Slurry ≈ 34 % solids → wet cake with ≈ 20–30 % water.

Dryer

Flash or fluid bed with hot air to below ≈ 0.3 % moisture.

Sieve, silo

Coarse fraction (lumps) removed; product stored and bagged.

Evaporating water costs ≈ 2.4 MJ/kg; a centrifuge removes it for a fraction of that.

Interactive — dryer water balance

What the centrifuge saves the dryer

$$\dot m_{evap}=\dot m_{PVC}\left(\frac{w_{in}}{1-w_{in}}-\frac{w_{out}}{1-w_{out}}\right)$$

$w$: water mass fraction of the wet PVC.

water evaporated, t/h

heat of evaporation

At 25 t/h PVC, every 5 % less cake water saves ≈ 2 t/h of evaporation: the centrifuge sets the dryer's energy.

Part 7 · summary

What Part 7 settled

  • Degassed and stripped VCM is compressed, condensed and reused.
  • Inerts carry VCM out of every condenser: keep air out.
  • Stripping to ppm needs a stripping factor well above 1.
  • Centrifuge first, dryer second: cake water sets drying energy.
  • Cooling water, air and power failures reach R-101 within minutes.

Graded procedure · limit 3 h

Cold start: empty, air-filled R-101 to a lined-out batch1 of 2

Objective: run the whole charge sequence through the permissives and initiate without overshoot.

  1. Jacket circulation on; baffle water AUTO 80 m³/h.
  2. Evacuate below 0.05 bar a; close XV-109.
  3. Charge 60 t water with the PVA pot open, then close it.
  4. Agitator running before the VCM charge.
  5. Charge 51 t VCM; stop P-103.

Graded procedure · limit 3 h

Cold start: heat-up, initiation, line-out2 of 2

  1. Heat up on steam to TI-100 ≥ 54 °C.
  2. TIC-100 AUTO 57 °C, TIC-110 in CASCADE.
  3. Charge the initiator (XV-103).
  4. LIC-100 AUTO 83 %, FIC-103 in CASCADE.
  5. E-101 in service via VPC-130 → FIC-130; inerts vented, HIC-135 back to 0 %.
  6. Hold 20 min at 57 ± 0.5 °C, no foam, no trip.

Zero if TI-101 exceeds 59 °C between 15 and 90 min after initiation.

Graded procedure · limit 2.5 h · starts 4.4 h into the reaction

End of batch

Objective: end the batch at the right moment and empty it without releasing VCM.

  1. Recognise the end point; inject short-stop.
  2. Stop the injection water (FIC-103 out of cascade, closed).
  3. Degas to VCM recovery below 2 bar g.
  4. Close XV-105; open the N₂ pad.
  5. Discharge with the agitator running; close valves when empty.

Graded procedures · from the 2 h batch

Three upsets to ride through

ProcedureObjectiveGraded steps (limit)
Jacket pump failsKeep the batch through a pump trip.spare on, flow > 400, in band, hold 5 min, report (25 min)
Initiator slugStop a runaway before the SIS does.see no margin, short-stop, T falling, inform (45 min)
Condenser upsetFind an unknown upset and restore E-101 duty.graded by the tracker once loaded (1 h)

Graded live · 45 min from the 2 h batch

Cooling-water optimisation

Objective: use less cooling water without losing temperature or margin.

Target at 45 min (2.5 points each)
TI-101 within 57 ± 0.3 °C
TV-110B ≤ 80 % and TI-131 ≤ 58 °C
Total cooling water ≤ 270 m³/h (design ≈ 330)
No alarm active or unacknowledged

What Part 8 settled

  • Training: 20 single faults — recognise, respond, recover.

  • Procedures: 6 graded runs — zero for any unsafe act.
  • Checks: what-if, trend matching, scrambles, reading sheet.

Before you open the console

Key Takeaways

1

Hold 57 ± 0.5 °C all batch: temperature sets the K-value.

2

Watch cooling margin — TV-110B and E-101 — not only temperature.

3

Read pressure as the phase signal: flat, then a 1.8 bar drop.

4

Short-stop early rather than let the SIS do it at 63 °C.

5

Cross-check every transmitter against a second, independent one.
